claim: Average serum level of LXA4 in posterior uveitis patients was significantly lower than in healthy subjects (p=0.0135).
source: Average serum level of LXA4 in patients were significantly lower than in healthy subjects (p=0.0135).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of serum LXA4 in 41 healthy subjects and 78 uveitis patients, with statistical significance shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Intermediate uveitis patients (n=5) had significantly lower serum LXA4 levels compared to healthy subjects (p=0.019).
source: However, differences between individual diagnoses and healthy subjects did not reach significance, except for the group of intermediate uveitis (n = 5, p=0.019).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 1A comparing specific uveitis diagnoses to healthy controls.

claim: LXA4 and its pathway markers (5-HETE and 15-HETE) were significantly elevated in eyes at peak disease (day 16) compared to naive unimmunized mice.
source: LXA4 and its 5-LOX and 12/15-LOX pathway markers (5-HETE and 15-HETE) were significantly elevated in eyes at peak disease compared to naive unimmunized mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS quantification of lipid mediators in eye tissue shown in Figure 1C.

claim: LXA4, 5-HETE and 15-HETE levels were significantly downregulated at peak disease in the inguinal lymph nodes.
source: By contrast, LXA4, 5-HETE and 15-HETE levels were significantly downregulated at peak disease in the inguinal lymph nodes (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 1B and 1C comparing naive and EAU-challenged mice.

claim: LXA4 levels did not change in the distal lymph nodes or eye-draining submandibular lymph nodes during EAU.
source: LXA4 levels did not change in the distal lymph nodes or eye-draining submandibular lymph nodes.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Serum LXA4 levels in EAU-challenged mice did not change compared to naïve mice.
source: While serum LXA4 levels in EAU-challenged mice did not change compared to naïve mice, pathway markers 5-LOX and 15-LOX showed significant and progressive decreases during EAU (naïve vs. EAU day 16, p=0.0078 and p=0.0048 for 5-HETE and 15-HETE respectively).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS analysis of serum samples shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Serum 5-HETE levels showed significant and progressive decreases during EAU (naïve vs. EAU day 16, p=0.0078).
source: While serum LXA4 levels in EAU-challenged mice did not change compared to naïve mice, pathway markers 5-LOX and 15-LOX showed significant and progressive decreases during EAU (naïve vs. EAU day 16, p=0.0078 and p=0.0048 for 5-HETE and 15-HETE respectively).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS analysis of serum samples shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Serum 15-HETE levels showed significant and progressive decreases during EAU (naïve vs. EAU day 16, p=0.0048).
source: While serum LXA4 levels in EAU-challenged mice did not change compared to naïve mice, pathway markers 5-LOX and 15-LOX showed significant and progressive decreases during EAU (naïve vs. EAU day 16, p=0.0078 and p=0.0048 for 5-HETE and 15-HETE respectively).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS analysis of serum samples shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LTB4 levels did not change significantly in inguinal lymph nodes during EAU pathogenesis.
source: However, unlike LXA4, LTB4 levels did not change significantly in inguinal lymph nodes during EAU pathogenesis.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Alox5 expression in the retina was upregulated by approximately five-fold on day 14 post-immunization compared to earlier time points and to naive mice.
source: In the retina, Alox5 expression was upregulated by approximately five-fold on day 14 post-immunization in comparison to earlier time points and to naive mice (Figure 1D), which directly correlated with upregulation of LXA4 formation in the eye.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Alox15 expression in the retina remained comparable to naïve mice during the entire time course of EAU.
source: Alox15 expression remained comparable to naïve mice during the entire time course of EAU, whereas Fpr2 expression changed throughout the time course of EAU, likely reflecting changes in circulating leukocytes populations that express varying levels of Fpr2 in the lymph node, and in temporal regulation of the homeostatic LXA4 pathway by resident cells in the retina.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Alox5 expression in inguinal lymph nodes was significantly upregulated on day 3 and day 14 post-immunization.
source: In the inguinal lymph nodes, Alox5 expression was significantly upregulated on day 3 and day 14 post-immunization, whereas Fpr2 expression was highly upregulated on day 3, but not on day 14 post-immunization (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Fpr2 expression in inguinal lymph nodes was highly upregulated on day 3, but not on day 14 post-immunization.
source: In the inguinal lymph nodes, Alox5 expression was significantly upregulated on day 3 and day 14 post-immunization, whereas Fpr2 expression was highly upregulated on day 3, but not on day 14 post-immunization (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Fpr2 expression on CD4+ T cells isolated from inguinal lymph nodes was significantly upregulated at peak disease compared to CD4+ T cells from naïve mice.
source: RNA expression of lipoxygenases (5-LOX and 12/15-LOX) demonstrates selective and temporal modulation of tissue-resident LXA4 pathway during EAU, while increased Fpr2 expression in CD4+ T cells in the inguinal lymph nodes potentiates their ability to interact with LXA4 during the effector phase of the immune response.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Disease scores of Alox5-/- mice were significantly higher than WT mice starting on day 16 post-immunization.
source: Disease scores of Alox5-/- mice were significantly higher than WT mice starting on day 16 post-immunization, and retinal inflammation in Alox5-/- persisted while inflammation gradually resolved in WT by day 20 post-immunization (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by fundoscopy scoring shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Visual function of immunized Alox5-/- mice was significantly impaired compared to WT mice.
source: Electroretinography showed that visual function of immunized Alox5-/- mice was significantly impaired compared to WT mice (Figure 2D), in line with the more severe disease phenotype in Alox5-/- mice.
evidence: Supported by electroretinography measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There were significantly more cell infiltrates including CD4+ T cells and CD4+ IFN-γ producing T cells in eyes of Alox5-/- mice than in WT mice on day 18 post-immunization.
source: Flow cytometric analyses of ocular infiltrating cells revealed that there were significantly more cell infiltrates including CD4+ T cells and CD4+ IFN-γ producing T cells in eyes of Alox5-/- mice than in WT mice on day 18 post-immunization (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: Lymphocytes from Alox5-/- mice exhibited higher antigen-specific proliferative responses to IRBP651-670 peptide than WT mice.
source: Lymphocytes from Alox5-/- mice exhibited higher antigen-specific proliferative responses to IRBP651-670 peptide than WT mice, as assessed by 3H thymidine-incorporation assay (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by 3H thymidine-incorporation assay shown in Figure 2G.

claim: LXA4-treated immunized mice developed significantly less disease compared to the vehicle-treated group.
source: LXA4-treated immunized mice developed significantly less disease compared to the vehicle-treated group (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by fundoscopy scores shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LXA4 treatment significantly reduced ocular infiltration of pathogenic IFN-γ and IL-17A producing CD4+ T cells.
source: Flow cytometry analyses of eyes harvested during peak inflammation confirmed that LXA4 treatment significantly reduced ocular infiltration of pathogenic IFN-γ and IL-17A producing CD4+ T cells (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: Antigen-specific recall responses of lymphocytes from inguinal lymph nodes of LXA4-treated mice were markedly decreased compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: In contrast, antigen-specific recall responses of lymphocytes from inguinal lymph nodes of LXA4-treated mice were markedly decreased (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay shown in Figure 3H.

claim: LXA4-treated mice developed significantly lower disease in a dose-dependent manner than vehicle-treated mice in adoptive transfer experiments.
source: LXA4-treated mice developed significantly lower disease in a dose-dependent manner than vehicle-treated mice (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by fundoscopy scores from adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 3I.

claim: LXA4 treatment downregulated expression of inflammatory markers Icam1, Il1b, Mapk1, Mapk3, Nfkb1, Ptgs2 (Cox-2), Tgfb, Tnfaip3, and Vcam1 in eyes during EAU.
source: Eyes of vehicle-treated mice exhibited increased expression of inflammatory markers Icam1, Il1b, Mapk1, Mapk3, Nfkb1, Ptgs2 (Cox-2), Tgfb, Tnfaip3, and Vcam1 in eyes, whereas LXA4 treatment downregulated the expression of these markers during EAU.
evidence: Supported by nanoString gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of inflammatory genes was comparable in the inguinal lymph nodes of vehicle vs. LXA4-treated animals.
source: By contrast, expression of these genes was comparable in the inguinal lymph nodes of vehicle vs. LXA4-treated animals (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by nanoString gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Eyes of LXA4 treated mice had downregulated expression of Ccr7, Cxcr3 and Ccl19 compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: Compared to vehicle- treated mice, eyes of LXA4 treated mice had downregulated expression of Ccr7, Cxcr3 and Ccl19 (Figure 4B), which paralleled the reduced numbers of total CD4+ T cells and CD4+ IFN-γ+ T cells in the ocular infiltrate (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by nanoString gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ccr7 and Ccl21a were highly upregulated in the inguinal lymph nodes of LXA4-treated mice compared to controls.
source: In contrast, Ccr7 and Ccl21a were highly upregulated in the inguinal lymph nodes of LXA4-treated mice compared to controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by nanoString gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LXA4 treatment downregulated expression of S1pr1 in the inguinal lymph nodes that drain the site of immunization, but not in the eye, submandibular lymph nodes, or distal lymph nodes.
source: LXA4 treatment downregulated expression of S1pr1 in the inguinal lymph nodes that drain the site of immunization, but not in the eye, submandibular lymph nodes that drain the eye, or distal lymph nodes (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: S1pr1 expression showed a trend of higher expression in CD4+ T cells from Alox5-/- mice compared to WT mice.
source: S1pr1 expression showed a trend of higher expression in CD4+ T cells from Alox5-/- mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Significantly higher numbers of CD4+ T cells from LXA4-deficient mice migrated toward CCL19 and CCL21 chemokine gradients than CD4+ T cells from WT mice.
source: Significantly higher numbers of CD4+ T cells from LXA4-deficient mice migrated toward CCL19 and CCL21 chemokine gradients than CD4+ T cells from WT mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by transwell migration assay shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CCR7 expression was modestly upregulated in a dose-dependent manner on in vitro stimulated T cells treated with LXA4.
source: CCR7 expression was modestly upregulated (Figure 4F) while S1PR1 expression was downregulated (Figure 4G) in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: S1PR1 expression was downregulated in a dose-dependent manner on in vitro stimulated T cells treated with LXA4.
source: CCR7 expression was modestly upregulated (Figure 4F) while S1PR1 expression was downregulated (Figure 4G) in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Recipients of Alox5-/- T cells developed more severe EAU, with more granulomatous lesions and damage in the photoreceptor cell layer, than recipients of WT T cells.
source: Consistent with the phenotype of exacerbated EAU in Alox5-/- mice (Figure 2), recipients of Alox5-/- T cells developed more severe EAU, with more granulomatous lesions and damage in the photoreceptor cell layer, than recipients of WT T cells (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by fundoscopy scores and histology shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Eyes of Alox5-/- T cell recipients had significantly more total ocular infiltrates, specifically total CD4+ T cells and IFN-γ producing CD4+ T cells than WT donor T cell recipients.
source: Eyes of Alox5-/- T cell recipients had significantly more total ocular infiltrates, specifically total CD4+ T cells and IFN-γ producing CD4+ T cells than WT donor T cell recipients (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The frequency of IFN-γ+ donor CD4+ T cells from Alox5-/- mice in inguinal lymph nodes was higher than that from WT.
source: In the inguinal lymph nodes, the frequency of IFN-γ+ donor CD4+ T cells from Alox5-/- mice, but not total or IL-17A+ donor CD4+ T cells, was higher than that from WT (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Migration marker analysis showed higher frequency of CXCR3+ in Alox5-/- donor CD4+ T cells in the inguinal lymph nodes.
source: Migration marker analysis showed higher frequency of CXCR3+ in Alox5-/- donor CD4+ T cells in the inguinal lymph nodes, whereas frequency of activated CD4+ CCR7+ donor T cells from Alox5-/- mice was significantly lower (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Frequency of activated CD4+ CCR7+ donor T cells from Alox5-/- mice was significantly lower than WT in inguinal lymph nodes.
source: Migration marker analysis showed higher frequency of CXCR3+ in Alox5-/- donor CD4+ T cells in the inguinal lymph nodes, whereas frequency of activated CD4+ CCR7+ donor T cells from Alox5-/- mice was significantly lower (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: CD4+ T cells from Alox5-/- mice achieved significantly higher glycoPER at baseline as well as after inhibition of the mitochondrial electron transport chain with rotenone and antimycin A.
source: CD4+ T cells from Alox5-/- mice achieved significantly higher glycoPER at baseline as well as after inhibition of the mitochondrial electron transport chain with rotenone and antimycin A (Rot/AA) (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse Glycolytic Rate Assay shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: LXA4 treated CD4+ T cells had significantly lower glycoPER at base line and after mitochondrial inhibition.
source: CD4+ T cells from WT mice were treated in vitro with LXA4 or vehicle control. LXA4 treated CD4+ T cells had significantly lower glycoPER at base line and after mitochondrial inhibition (Figure 6D), as well as lower basal (Figure 6E) and compensatory (Figure 6F) glycolysis.
evidence: Supported by Seahorse Glycolytic Rate Assay shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: LXA4 treated CD4+ T cells had lower basal and compensatory glycolysis.
source: CD4+ T cells from WT mice were treated in vitro with LXA4 or vehicle control. LXA4 treated CD4+ T cells had significantly lower glycoPER at base line and after mitochondrial inhibition (Figure 6D), as well as lower basal (Figure 6E) and compensatory (Figure 6F) glycolysis.
evidence: Supported by Seahorse Glycolytic Rate Assay shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: Posterior autoimmune uveitis accounts for 10–15% of blindness in the Western world and primarily affects working age adults.
source: Posterior autoimmune uveitis accounts for 10–15% of blindness in the Western world and primarily affects working age adults (Durrani et al., 2004; Gritz and Wong, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Durrani et al., 2004 and Gritz and Wong, 2004.

claim: Autoimmune uveitis is mediated by pathogenic Th1 and Th17 responses to retina-specific antigens, such as interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP) and retinal arrestin.
source: Autoimmune uveitis is mediated by pathogenic Th1 and Th17 responses to retina-specific antigens, such as interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP) and retinal arrestin.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of autoimmune uveitis pathogenesis.

claim: Upon peripheral immunization with retinal antigens in complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA), T cells are primed in the inguinal lymph nodes that drain the immunization sites.
source: Upon peripheral immunization with retinal antigens in complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA), T cells are primed in the inguinal lymph nodes that drain the immunization sites. Activated retina-specific T cells then traffic to the eye and elicit inflammation that starts 9–11 days and peaks 14–16 days after immunization (Caspi, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caspi, 2010 describing EAU model.

claim: Activated retina-specific T cells traffic to the eye and elicit inflammation that starts 9–11 days and peaks 14–16 days after immunization.
source: Activated retina-specific T cells then traffic to the eye and elicit inflammation that starts 9–11 days and peaks 14–16 days after immunization (Caspi, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caspi, 2010 describing EAU model.

claim: LXA4 is an endogenous arachidonic acid-derived signaling molecule that exerts anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving activities via formyl peptide receptor 2 (ALX/FPR2) in mice and humans.
source: LXA4 is an endogenous arachidonic acid-derived signaling molecule that exerts anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving activities via formyl peptide receptor 2 (ALX/FPR2) in mice and humans.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of LXA4 biochemistry and signaling.

claim: 5-LOX is the only enzyme in mammals that can generate the 5,6 epoxide intermediate leukotriene A4 required for the formation of LXA4 and other epoxide intermediates of several specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs).
source: 5-LOX is the only enzyme in mammals that can generate the 5,6 epoxide intermediate leukotriene A4 required for the formation of LXA4 and other epoxide intermediates of several specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs) (Wei and Gronert, 2017; Serhan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wei and Gronert, 2017 and Serhan, 2014.

claim: 5-LOX in the retina has protective roles.
source: Even though 5-LOX also initiates the generation of pro-inflammatory leukotrienes by leukocytes, 5-LOX in the retina has protective roles (Sapieha et al., 2011; Livne-Bar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sapieha et al., 2011 and Livne-Bar et al., 2017.

claim: LXA4 is an important tissue-resident pathway in eyes and draining lymph nodes that controls ocular surface inflammation and immune responses, and it is neuroprotective in the retina.
source: Emerging evidence indicates that LXA4 is an important tissue-resident pathway in eyes and draining lymph nodes that controls ocular surface inflammation and immune responses, and it is neuroprotective in the retina (Wei and Gronert, 2017; Livne-Bar et al., 2017; Kenchegowda and Bazan, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wei and Gronert, 2017; Livne-Bar et al., 2017; and Kenchegowda and Bazan, 2010.

claim: The defining functions of LXA4 include inhibition of neutrophil infiltration to the site of inflammation, promotion of macrophage efferocytosis, and reduction of inflammatory cytokine and chemokine production.
source: The defining functions of LXA4 include inhibition of neutrophil infiltration to the site of inflammation, promotion of macrophage efferocytosis, and reduction of inflammatory cytokine and chemokine production (Serhan, 2014; Serhan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Serhan, 2014 and Serhan et al., 2008.

claim: In vitro studies demonstrated that LXA4 and SPMs have a role in T follicular and helper cell differentiation.
source: In vitro studies demonstrated that LXA4 and SPMs have a role in T follicular and helper cell differentiation (Nagaya et al., 2017; Chiurchiù et al., 2016), and neutrophil-derived LXA4 was previously shown to inhibit T effector cell responses in lymph nodes in immune-driven dry eye disease (Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nagaya et al., 2017 and Chiurchiù et al., 2016.

claim: Neutrophil-derived LXA4 was previously shown to inhibit T effector cell responses in lymph nodes in immune-driven dry eye disease.
source: In vitro studies demonstrated that LXA4 and SPMs have a role in T follicular and helper cell differentiation (Nagaya et al., 2017; Chiurchiù et al., 2016), and neutrophil-derived LXA4 was previously shown to inhibit T effector cell responses in lymph nodes in immune-driven dry eye disease (Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao et al., 2015.

claim: ALX/FPR2 is expressed on T cells.
source: ALX/FPR2 is expressed on T cells (Ariel et al., 2003), providing a modality for LXA4 regulation of adaptive immunity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ariel et al., 2003.

claim: Changes of SPMs in human blood have been proposed as diagnostic markers of health and disease outcomes.
source: Changes of SPMs in human blood have been proposed as diagnostic markers of health and disease outcomes (Colas et al., 2014; Norris et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colas et al., 2014 and Norris et al., 2018.

claim: Alox5-/- mice are LXA4 deficient.
source: Alox5-/- mice are LXA4 deficient (Aliberti et al., 2002), since 5-LOX is a necessary enzyme required for LXA4 biosynthesis (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aliberti et al., 2002 and LC-MS/MS data in Figure 2A.

claim: There are no reports of compensatory upregulation of other eicosanoid pathways (cyclooxygenases, 12-LOX or 15-LOX) in the Alox5-/- mouse line.
source: There are no reports of compensatory upregulation of other eicosanoid pathways (cyclooxygenases, 12-LOX or 15-LOX) in this mouse line.
evidence: Based on review of literature on Alox5-/- mice.

claim: Th1 and Th17 are T cell subsets that drive EAU pathogenesis.
source: Th1 and Th17 are T cell subsets that drive EAU pathogenesis (Damsker et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Damsker et al., 2010.

claim: The S1PR1-sphingosine-1 phosphate axis is a primary mechanism for regulating lymph node T cell egress and lymphocyte recirculation.
source: The S1PR1-sphingosine-1 phosphate axis is a primary mechanism for regulating lymph node T cell egress and lymphocyte recirculation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of lymphocyte trafficking.

claim: Pharmacological downregulation of S1PR1 prevents trafficking of autoreactive T cells and is an FDA-approved treatment for multiple sclerosis.
source: Pharmacological downregulation of S1PR1 prevents trafficking of autoreactive T cells and is an FDA-approved treatment for multiple sclerosis (Garris et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garris et al., 2014.

claim: The CCR7-CCL19/CCL21 axis facilitates naïve T cell homing to secondary lymphoid organs, activated T cell egress, and the interaction between T cells and dendritic cells (DC) to induce peripheral tolerance or to elicit an adaptive immune response.
source: The CCR7-CCL19/CCL21 axis facilitates naïve T cell homing to secondary lymphoid organs, activated T cell egress, and the interaction between T cells and dendritic cells (DC) to induce peripheral tolerance or to elicit an adaptive immune response (Comerford et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Comerford et al., 2013.

claim: T cell glycolysis is vital in regulating T cell effector function.
source: T cell glycolysis is vital in regulating T cell effector function. Metabolic switch from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis is required to sustain T effector function and cytokine production (Coe et al., 2014; Salmond, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coe et al., 2014 and Salmond, 2018.

claim: Metabolic switch from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis is required to sustain T effector function and cytokine production.
source: Metabolic switch from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis is required to sustain T effector function and cytokine production (Coe et al., 2014; Salmond, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coe et al., 2014 and Salmond, 2018.

claim: Inhibition of glycolysis abrogates IFN-γ production in activated CD4+ T cells, implicating glycolysis as regulator of sustained T effector responses.
source: Inhibition of glycolysis abrogates IFN-γ production in activated CD4+ T cells, implicating glycolysis as regulator of sustained T effector responses (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2013.

claim: T cell glycolysis and mitochondrial metabolism as potential therapeutic targets are supported by elevated glycolytic metabolism in T cells of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients and reduced IFN-γ production and disease biomarkers upon inhibition of CD4+ T cell glycolysis in mouse models of SLE.
source: T cell glycolysis and mitochondrial metabolism as potential therapeutic targets are supported by elevated glycolytic metabolism in T cells of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients and reduced IFN-γ production and disease biomarkers upon inhibition of CD4+ T cell glycolysis in mouse models of SLE (Yin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yin et al., 2015.

claim: In mice and humans, LXA4 cognate receptor ALX/FPR2 is expressed in T cells, B cells and innate lymphoid cells.
source: In mice and humans, LXA4 cognate receptor ALX/FPR2 is expressed in T cells, B cells and innate lymphoid cells (Wei and Gronert, 2019), and has been shown to regulate CD4+ T cell cytokine production in vitro (Chiurchiù et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wei and Gronert, 2019 and Chiurchiù et al., 2016.

claim: ALX/FPR2 has been shown to regulate CD4+ T cell cytokine production in vitro.
source: In mice and humans, LXA4 cognate receptor ALX/FPR2 is expressed in T cells, B cells and innate lymphoid cells (Wei and Gronert, 2019), and has been shown to regulate CD4+ T cell cytokine production in vitro (Chiurchiù et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chiurchiù et al., 2016.

claim: A second LXA4 receptor GPR32 has been identified in humans, which currently has no mouse homolog.
source: A second LXA4 receptor GPR32 has been identified in humans (Dalli and Serhan, 2019), which currently has no mouse homolog.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dalli and Serhan, 2019.

claim: EAU is an induced and well characterized model of autoimmune uveitis that recapitulates features of human posterior autoimmune uveitis.
source: EAU is an induced and well characterized model of autoimmune uveitis that recapitulates features of human posterior autoimmune uveitis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the EAU model.

claim: LXA4 has been identified as an abundant SPM in human axillary lymph nodes.
source: Although the immune-regulatory roles of LXA4 in human draining lymph nodes remain to be defined, LXA4 has been identified as an abundant SPM in human axillary lymph nodes (Colas et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Colas et al., 2014.

claim: There are significant differences in mouse and human immune responses.
source: While it is important to note that there are significant differences in mouse and human immune responses (Seok et al., 2013), LXA4 pathway and receptors are conserved in humans and mice and are targeted as novel therapies based on promising results from animal studies.
evidence: Supported by citation to Seok et al., 2013.

claim: LXA4 pathway and receptors are conserved in humans and mice.
source: While it is important to note that there are significant differences in mouse and human immune responses (Seok et al., 2013), LXA4 pathway and receptors are conserved in humans and mice and are targeted as novel therapies based on promising results from animal studies.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of LXA4 biochemistry across species.

claim: Prevalence of autoimmunity has increased steadfastly in recent decades.
source: Understanding the development of adaptive immune responses to self-antigens is imperative, as prevalence of autoimmunity has increased steadfastly in recent decades (Lerner and Matthias, 2015; Bach, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lerner and Matthias, 2015 and Bach, 2002.

claim: Downregulation of the basal tone of LXA4 in draining lymph nodes is a key feature of developing adaptive immunity in EAU.
source: Our data indicate that downregulated endogenous LXA4, specifically in inguinal lymph nodes that drain the immunization site, is a key feature of developing adaptive immunity, that is EAU.
evidence: Inferred from the observed selective downregulation of LXA4 in inguinal lymph nodes during EAU development shown in Figure 1.

claim: The lymph node resident LXA4 pathway is a significant checkpoint in the development and severity of adaptive immunity.
source: Our results demonstrate the intrinsic lymph node LXA4 pathway as a significant checkpoint in the development and severity of adaptive immunity.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental findings showing LXA4 regulation of T cell function, trafficking, and metabolism.

claim: LXA4 regulates T cell effector function and trafficking through modulation of CCR7 and S1PR1 expression and glucose metabolism in CD4+ T cells.
source: In vivo deletion or supplementation of LXA4 identified modulation of CC-chemokine receptor 7 (CCR7) and sphingosine 1- phosphate receptor-1 (S1PR1) expression and glucose metabolism in CD4+ T cells as potential mechanisms for LXA4 regulation of T cell effector function and trafficking.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LXA4 treatment and Alox5-/- mice showing changes in CCR7, S1PR1, and glycolysis.

claim: Amplification of the resident lymph node LXA4 pathway may be a potential target to prevent the development of pathogenic adaptive immune responses and autoimmunity.
source: Thus, amplification of the resident lymph node LXA4 pathway may be a potential target to prevent the development of pathogenic adaptive immune responses and autoimmunity.
evidence: Based on the demonstrated protective effects of LXA4 treatment and detrimental effects of LXA4 deficiency in EAU.

claim: LXA4 acts directly on T cells and modulates trafficking through regulation of S1PR1 and CCR7 expression.
source: Together, these data are compatible with the interpretation that LXA4 acts directly on T cells and modulates trafficking through regulation of S1PR1 and CCR7 expression.
evidence: Supported by in vitro experiments showing dose-dependent effects of LXA4 on S1PR1 and CCR7 expression in T cells.

claim: The downregulation of CCR7 expression and increased ocular infiltration of CD4+ T cells support the hypothesis that egress of effector T cells from inguinal draining lymph nodes is augmented in LXA4-deficient mice.
source: The downregulation of CCR7 expression and increased ocular infiltration of CD4+ T cells support the hypothesis that egress of effector T cells from inguinal draining lymph nodes is augmented in LXA4-deficient mice.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data showing lower CCR7 expression and higher ocular infiltration in Alox5-/- T cell recipients.

claim: The ability of LXA4 to downregulate glycolysis in activated CD4+ T cell suggests that the lymph node resident LXA4 pathway is a potential checkpoint to limit inflammatory cytokine production and the magnitude of adaptive immune responses.
source: The ability of LXA4 to downregulate glycolysis in activated CD4+ T cell is of interest and suggests that the lymph node resident LXA4 pathway is a potential checkpoint to limit inflammatory cytokine production and the magnitude of adaptive immune responses.
evidence: Based on Seahorse metabolic assay data showing LXA4 reduces glycolysis in CD4+ T cells.

claim: Increased capacity of LXA4 signaling in T cells is a counter-regulatory mechanism in response to the development of adaptive immunity.
source: During peak EAU, Fpr2 expression in CD4+ T cells was highly upregulated in the inguinal lymph nodes that drain the site of immunization, suggesting that increased capacity of LXA4 signaling in T cells is a counter-regulatory mechanism in response to the development of adaptive immunity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Fpr2 expression increases during peak EAU in CD4+ T cells.

claim: Incomplete abrogation of LXA4 signaling due to a putative second receptor may explain why immunized global Fpr2-/- mice did not develop more severe autoimmune disease.
source: Our data suggest that additional receptors for LXA4 may exist in mice. Incomplete abrogation of LXA4 signaling due to a putative second receptor may explain why immunized global Fpr2-/- mice did not develop more severe autoimmune disease.
evidence: Based on the observation that Fpr2-/- mice did not show exacerbated EAU unlike Alox5-/- mice, despite adoptive transfer of Fpr2-/- T cells causing more severe disease.

claim: Systemic LXA4 treatment reduced expression of inflammatory genes in the effector site (eyes), but not in the inductive site (lymph nodes draining the site of immunization).
source: These data suggest that systemic LXA4 treatment reduced expression of inflammatory genes in the effector site, that is eyes, but not in the inductive site, that is lymph nodes draining the site of immunization.
evidence: Based on nanoString gene expression analysis comparing eyes and inguinal lymph nodes from LXA4-treated vs vehicle-treated mice.

claim: LXA4 provides direct evidence that it inhibits the actions of antigen-primed lymphocytes in vivo and also regulates the effector phase of the adaptive immune response.
source: These findings provide direct evidence that LXA4 inhibits the actions of antigen-primed lymphocytes in vivo and also regulates the effector phase of the adaptive immune response.
evidence: Based on adoptive transfer experiments showing LXA4 treatment reduces disease severity in a dose-dependent manner.

claim: Both ex vivo evidence from CD4+ T cells of EAU-challenged LXA4-deficient mice and in vitro experiments of LXA4-treated CD4+ WT T cells indicate that lymph node resident LXA4 has a direct role in regulating metabolic functions of CD4+ T cells.
source: Thus, both ex vivo evidence from CD4+ T cells of EAU-challenged LXA4-deficient mice and in vitro experiments of LXA4-treated CD4+ WT T cells indicate that lymph node resident LXA4 has a direct role in regulating metabolic functions of CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Based on Seahorse metabolic assays showing increased glycolysis in Alox5-/- T cells and decreased glycolysis with LXA4 treatment.

claim: The overall decrease in serum LXA4 level in patients suggests that the LXA4 pathway is physiologically relevant during pathogenesis of posterior segment uveitis.
source: The overall decrease in serum LXA4 level in patients suggests that the LXA4 pathway is physiologically relevant during pathogenesis of posterior segment uveitis.
evidence: Based on ELISA measurements showing lower serum LXA4 in uveitis patients compared to healthy controls.

claim: Increased RNA levels of Alox5 in inguinal lymph nodes did not correlate with 5-LOX activity and LXA4 production as both 5-HETE and LXA4 levels were decreased on day 10 and day 16.
source: Increased RNA levels of Alox5 in inguinal lymph nodes did not correlate with 5-LOX activity and LXA4 production as both 5-HETE and LXA4 levels were decreased on day 10 and day 16 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on comparison of RT-PCR data for Alox5 expression and LC-MS/MS data for LXA4 and 5-HETE levels.

claim: Transferred T cells from Fpr2-/- and Alox5-/- mice induced different signatures of inflammatory ocular infiltrates, likely due to differential regulation of donor T cells and innate effector cells by the host LXA4 pathway in TCRb-/- recipient mice.
source: Transferred T cells from Fpr2-/- and Alox5-/- mice induced different signatures of inflammatory ocular infiltrates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C), likely due to differential regulation of donor T cells and innate effector cells by the host LXA4 pathway in TCRb-/- recipient mice.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry analysis of ocular infiltrates in TCRb-/- recipients of Fpr2-/- vs Alox5-/- T cells.

claim: LXA4 treatment reduced the number of CD4+ T cells and the level of COX-2 expression in the eye compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: In LXA4-treated mice, the number of CD4+ T cells and the level of COX-2 expression were significantly reduced in comparison to vehicle-treated mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 3E.

claim: COX-2 localization was observed in the outer plexiform, choroid, retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor layers of the eye during EAU.
source: Immunohistochemistry revealed COX-2 localization in the outer plexiform, choroid, retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor layers of the eye, while CD4+ T cell infiltration was observed in the choroid, RPE and into the photoreceptor layers (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CD4+ T cell infiltration was observed in the choroid, RPE and into the photoreceptor layers during EAU.
source: Immunohistochemistry revealed COX-2 localization in the outer plexiform, choroid, retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor layers of the eye, while CD4+ T cell infiltration was observed in the choroid, RPE and into the photoreceptor layers (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was no apparent difference in expression of the trafficking markers CXCR3, CCR6 and CCR7 by T cells that had infiltrated the eye in TCRb-/- recipients of WT vs Alox5-/- T cells.
source: However, there was no apparent difference in expression of the trafficking markers CXCR3, CCR6 and CCR7 by T cells that had infiltrated the eye (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Lipidomic analysis did not detect significant differences in basal levels of 12-HETE, 15-HETE, PGD2, PGE2, or TXB2 in inguinal lymph nodes of Alox5-/- mice.
source: Lipidomic analysis did not detect significant differences in basal levels of 12-HETE, 15-HETE, prostaglandin D2 (PGD2), prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), or thromboxane B2 (TXB2) in inguinal lymph nodes of Alox5-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Low amounts of 5-HETE and LXA4 were detected in Alox5-/- mice.
source: Low amounts of 5-HETE and LXA4 were detected in Alox5-/- mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS chromatograms shown in Figure 2A.

claim: It is possible that one of the other mouse lipoxygenase enzymes, which do not exist in humans (e.g. 8-LOX), is able to catalyze LXA4 formation in mice with low efficiency.
source: It is possible that one of the other mouse lipoxygenase enzymes, which do not exist in humans (e.g. 8-LOX), is able to catalyze LXA4 formation in mice with low efficiency.
evidence: Speculation based on the detection of low levels of LXA4 in Alox5-/- mice.

claim: Pathway markers for DHA-derived SPMs (4-HDHA, 7-HDHA, 14-HDHA and 17-HDHA) were detected in all tissues analyzed.
source: Pathway markers for DHA-derived SPMs (4-HDHA, 7-HDHA, 14-HDHA and 17-HDHA) were detected in all tissues, but DHA- or EPA- derived SPMs were not robustly detected or were below the signal-to-noise threshold (5:1) in our method.
evidence: Based on LC-MS/MS lipidomic analysis.

claim: DHA- or EPA-derived SPMs were not robustly detected or were below the signal-to-noise threshold (5:1) in the lipidomic analysis method.
source: Pathway markers for DHA-derived SPMs (4-HDHA, 7-HDHA, 14-HDHA and 17-HDHA) were detected in all tissues, but DHA- or EPA- derived SPMs were not robustly detected or were below the signal-to-noise threshold (5:1) in our method.
evidence: Based on LC-MS/MS lipidomic analysis.

claim: The finding that LTB4 levels did not change in inguinal lymph nodes during EAU is consistent with previous lipidomic analysis that identified changes in LXA4, but not LTB4, in eye draining lymph nodes of an immune-driven dry eye disease model.
source: The finding is consistent with our previous lipidomic analysis that identified changes in LXA4, but not LTB4, in eye draining lymph nodes of an immune-driven dry eye disease model (Gao et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gao et al., 2015 and Gao et al., 2018.

claim: Several research groups have established that tail vein, intraperitoneal, subcutaneous or subconjunctival injections of LXA4 or other SPMs (10 ng-1 μg) in mouse disease models induce long-lasting protective actions through changes in lymphocyte and neutrophil function and macrophage phenotype at distant tissue sites.
source: However, several research groups have established that tail vein, intraperitoneal, subcutaneous or subconjunctival injections of LXA4 or other SPMs (10 ng-1 μg) in mouse disease models induce long-lasting protective actions through changes in lymphocyte and neutrophil function and macrophage phenotype at distant tissue sites (Livne-Bar et al., 2017; Serhan et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2015; Fosshaug et al., 2019; Wei and Gronert, 2019), which indicate direct actions at the target tissue.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies: Livne-Bar et al., 2017; Serhan et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2015; Fosshaug et al., 2019; Wei and Gronert, 2019.

claim: Beneficial anti-inflammatory effects of LXA4 have been previously reported in the LPS-induced anterior uveitis model.
source: Beneficial anti-inflammatory effects of LXA4 have been previously reported in the LPS-induced anterior uveitis model, however, pathogenesis of LPS-induced uveitis is driven exclusively by innate immune responses (Karim et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Karim et al., 2009.

claim: In a murine asthma model induced by allergen immunization, LXA4 treatment reduced airway inflammation by increasing natural killer cell-mediated eosinophil apoptosis.
source: In a murine asthma model induced by allergen immunization, LXA4 treatment reduced airway inflammation by increasing natural killer cell-mediated eosinophil apoptosis (Barnig et al., 2013), demonstrating LXA4 regulation of innate responses in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citation to Barnig et al., 2013.

claim: Downregulated endogenous LXA4 in inguinal lymph nodes is consistent with a previous report which linked lower LXA4 levels in draining lymph nodes to exacerbated dry eye disease in female mice.
source: This is consistent with a previous report, which linked lower LXA4 levels in draining lymph nodes to exacerbated dry eye disease in female mice (Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao et al., 2015.
